passages.title: The oath by the charging war horses
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

These five ayat are a single sworn oath. Allah swears by the war-horses and by what they do in battle, and the oath is building towards what it is sworn about: that man is deeply ungrateful to his Lord (ayah 6). As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the hard tasks of the war-horses are called to bear testimony to the fact that man is very ungrateful for Allah's favours. The horses are not the point; they are the witness called to the stand.

**Where it was revealed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, on the authority of Qurtubi, that the scholars differed: Sayyidnā Ibn Masʿūd, Jābir, Ḥasan Baṣrī, ʿIkramah and ʿAṭāʾ held that Sūrah al-ʿĀdiyāt was revealed in Makkah, while Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās, Anas, Imām Mālik and Qatādah held it was revealed in Madinah. Both positions are transmitted; neither is settled here.

## Why Allah swears at all

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on something a reader can easily rush past. It is the prerogative of Allah to swear an oath by any of His creatures, whether to recount an event or to lay down ordinances. It is not permitted for any human being to take an oath by any created thing. The purpose of swearing an oath is to confirm, or give weight to, the truth stated after it. And when the Qurʼān swears by an object, that object has some *nexus* — some real connection — with the subject being sworn to.

So the question to hold in mind through all five ayat is: **what do galloping horses have to do with human ingratitude?** The sūrah answers it, but only after it has made you watch them.

## The charge, image by image

**Ayah 1 — وَٱلۡعَٰدِيَٰتِ ضَبۡحٗا, "By the galloping, panting horses."** *ʿĀdiyāt* is derived from the root *ʿadw*, which means "to run" (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). *Ḍabḥ* is the word that puts you beside the animal: it means "the sound coming out of the chest of a horse when it runs fast and breathes laboriously; panting." Ibn Kathir explains that Allah swears by the horses when they are made to gallop into battle in His path — that is, in jihād — "and thus they run and pant, which is the sound that is heard from the horse when it runs." The oath does not open with the rider, or the sword, or the victory. It opens with a labouring chest.

**Ayah 2 — فَٱلۡمُورِيَٰتِ قَدۡحٗا, "striking sparks of fire."** *Mūriyāt* is the active participle — the "doing" form of the word — from the infinitive *īrāʾ*, which means "to strike or produce fire with a particular piece of wood." *Qadḥ* means "to strike or produce fire with a flint," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies the picture intended here: the sparks struck when the horse runs fast on rocky ground with horse-shoes on. Ibn Kathir gives the same: "the striking of their hooves on the rocks, which causes sparks of fire to fly from them." The ground is stone, and the animal is running fast enough over it to set sparks flying.

**Ayah 3 — فَٱلۡمُغِيرَٰتِ صُبۡحٗا, "launching raids at dawn."** *Mughīrāt* is the active participle of the infinitive *ighārah*, which means "to attack, or make a sudden hostile excursion upon, an enemy." *Ṣubḥ* means "morning or dawn." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why this hour is named: it was the practice of the Arabs to attack their enemy at dawn rather than at night, in order to show their bravery — they considered a hostile excursion made under cover of darkness an act of cowardice. Ibn Kathir records that Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Qatādah all said this means "the invasion of the horses in the morning in the way of Allah."

**Ayah 4 — فَأَثَرۡنَ بِهِۦ نَقۡعٗا, "stirring up clouds of dust."** *Atharna* is derived from *ithārah*, which means "to raise dust," and *naqʿ* means "dust" (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). The observation there is exact: the dust is stirred up and spread upon the horizon — and morning is not normally the time for clouds of dust to fly in this way, unless it was caused by very fast running. Ibn Kathir keeps it simple: this is the dust at the place of the battle, raised by the horses; it is the place in which the attack takes place, and the dust is stirred up by it.

**Ayah 5 — فَوَسَطۡنَ بِهِۦ جَمۡعًا, "and penetrating into the heart of enemy lines."** Ibn Kathir explains that they are then all in the middle of that spot, together; and al-ʿAwfī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrimah, Qatādah and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk that they all said this means "into the midst of the disbelieving enemy." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the detail that makes ayah 5 the climax: they penetrate into the centre of the enemy forces **without the least degree of fear.**

## The Prophet's ﷺ practice at dawn

Ibn Kathir, commenting on the dawn raid of ayah 3, notes that this was the practice of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: he used to perform raids in the early morning, and he would wait to see whether he heard the adhān — the call to prayer — from the people. **If he heard it he would leave them alone; if he did not hear it, he would attack.**

(The bundle relates this as the Prophet's ﷺ practice without naming a hadith collection, so it is passed on here exactly as Ibn Kathir gives it, and attributed to no collection.)

There is something worth sitting with in that. The most fearsome image in the sūrah — cavalry at dawn — could be called off by a single sound: the voice of someone calling people to prayer.

## The point of the oath: the horse shames the man

Ibn Kathir titles his commentary on this sūrah "Swearing by the Horses of War about the Ungratefulness of Man and His Zeal for Wealth." The oath of ayat 1–5 exists to carry the weight of what follows it in ayah 6: *Verily, man is ungrateful to his Lord.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the connection out, and it is the single most illuminating thing in these five ayat. Look hard at what the horse is being asked to do. Man needs to look at the horses — especially the war-horses, who risk their lives travelling under very dangerous and difficult conditions, above all on the battlefield, where they follow the commands of their masters. It runs until its chest heaves. It strikes stone until sparks fly. It drives into the centre of an armed enemy without the least degree of fear. And it does all of this for a master who **did not create it**, and did not create so much as the fodder he feeds it. Man's task is merely to hand over fodder that Allah has created. For that small kindness the horses recognise and acknowledge the favour, and are prepared to risk their lives and bear the greatest of hardships.

Now turn the comparison around, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does. Allah created man from an insignificant drop of sperm and endowed him with high faculties, abilities, intellect and senses to perform every kind of task, thus making him the crown of His creation. He provided him with all types of food, and facilities are created for all his needs and necessities in an amazing manner. But man does not recognise or acknowledge any of these sublime favours, nor does he express his gratitude to his Creator.

That is the *nexus* the oath was built on. The Qurʼān does not argue the point abstractly. It puts a panting, fearless animal in front of you and lets the contrast do the work.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out three distinct steps, and it is worth taking them one at a time, because a person can fail at any one of them: man does not **recognise** Allah's favours, does not **acknowledge** them, and does not **thank** his Creator for them.

Recognising is seeing that what you have is a gift and not a given. Acknowledging is admitting, to yourself and out loud, where it came from. Thanking is what you then do about it. The horse manages all three for a handful of fodder that its master merely handed over. So the honest question these five ayat leave with us is not military at all: for existence itself, for intellect and senses, for food and for the astonishing arrangement of every need we have — where in those three steps do we stop?

passages.title: Humankind's ingratitude and love of wealth
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Five ayat of oaths sworn by charging war-horses lead up to a statement, and ayat 6–8 are that statement: a diagnosis of the human heart in three strokes — **man is ungrateful to his Lord (6), this is witnessed (7), and his love of wealth is fierce (8)**. What holds them together is that they are one sentence about one patient. Ingratitude is the disease; the intense grip of wealth on the heart is the symptom that makes the disease visible; and between them stands the ayah of witnessing, which says: this is not a hidden accusation, it is testified to.

## The statement the oath was building to

Of ayah 6, Ibn Kathir says plainly: "This is the subject what is being sworn about." Everything in the preceding oaths has been building pressure toward this line — which is why Ibn Kathir titles the whole passage "Swearing by the Horses of War about the Ungratefulness of Man and His Zeal for Wealth." The verdict on man lands with the full weight of the oath behind it: *inna al-insāna li-rabbihi la-kanūd*.

## "To his Lord" — the sting in the phrasing

Notice the ayah does not merely say man is ungrateful. It says he is ungrateful **to his Lord** — *li-rabbihi*. Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: "he (man) is ungrateful for the favors of His Lord and he rejects them." The ingratitude is not an abstract character flaw; it is directed at the very One who sustains and provides for him. The favours and the Giver are named in the same breath as the refusal.

## Kanūd: what the word carries

The word the Qur'an chooses is *kanūd*, and it is worth slowing down over, because the early authorities returned to it again and again.

**The agreed meaning.** Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ibrahim An-Nakhaʿi, Abu Al-Jawzaʼ, Abu Al-ʿAliyah, Abu Ad-Duha, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Muhammad bin Qays, Ad-Dahhak, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas and Ibn Zayd **all said**: "Al-Kanud means ungrateful." That is an unusually broad line-up for a single word, and it settles the core sense.

**But then the definitions get sharper.** Around that agreed core, several early figures described *what ingratitude actually looks like from the inside* — and this is where the ayah stops being a label and starts being a mirror:

- **Al-Hasan**, quoted by Ibn Kathir: "Al-Kanud is the one who counts the calamities (that befall him) and he forgets Allah's favors." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same definition, attributing it to Hasan Basri. A running tally of grievances; a blank page where the blessings should be.
- **Abu Bakr Wasiti**, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: *kanūd* is the one who spends the bounties of Allah for sinful purposes — taking the gift and turning it against the Giver.
- **Tirmidhi**, whose saying Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates: *kanūd* is "the one who looks at the bounty, and not at the Bounteous Lord" — so absorbed in the gift that he never lifts his eyes to the One who gave it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws the strands together: "all these interpretations lead to the sense of 'ungratefulness to favours and bounties' and hence the expression kanud means 'ungrateful'." They are not competing definitions but three angles on one condition.

Sit with Al-Hasan's description in particular. It describes a man who has an excellent memory — for the wrong ledger. He can recite every hardship of the past year and cannot name three mercies from this morning. That is *kanūd*, and it is a condition most of us will recognise before we finish reading the sentence.

## Ayah 7: who is the witness?

*Wa innahu ʿalā dhālika la-shahīd* — Ibn Kathir renders it, "And to that He bears witness." The Arabic pronoun is unspecified, and the commentators genuinely differed over who it refers to. Ibn Kathir preserves both readings without dismissing either:

**First view — the witness is Allah.** Qatadah and Sufyan Ath-Thawri both said: "And indeed Allah is a witness to that." On this reading, ayah 7 seals ayah 6. The charge of ingratitude is not a guess about human nature; it is testified to by the One who misses nothing.

**Second view — the witness is man himself.** Ibn Kathir says it is "also possible that the pronoun (He) could be referring to man," a view he attributes to **Muhammad bin Kaʿb Al-Qurazi**. The meaning would then be that man is a witness himself to the fact that he is ungrateful — and Ibn Kathir adds that "this is obvious in his condition," that is, apparent from his own statements and deeds. He supports it with a parallel from the Qur'an, where Allah says of the idolaters that it is not for them to maintain the Masajid of Allah "while they witness disbelief against themselves" (9:17).

That second reading is quietly devastating. It means no external prosecution is required. A person's own speech — the complaining, the sense of entitlement, the way he talks about what he has and what he is owed — files the testimony on his behalf.

## Ayah 8: "and he is fierce in the love of khayr"

*Wa innahu li-ḥubbi-l-khayri la-shadīd.*

**The word *khayr* here means wealth.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains: literally *khair* means "any good thing," but idiomatically in Arabic it means "wealth," the idiom implying that wealth is an embodiment of goodness and benefit. It notes the same usage elsewhere in the Qur'an, in the ayah of bequest (2:180) — "...he leaves some wealth..." — where again the word is *khair*. Ibn Kathir renders it the same way: "his love of the good, which is wealth."

There is already a gentle irony sitting inside the word. Man calls it *khayr*, "the good" — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān immediately qualifies that some type of wealth can involve man in untold misery, that in the Hereafter this will be the position of all wealth acquired through unlawful means, and that sometimes wealth in this world too can prove to be a nuisance and a disaster. The thing he is fierce for is named by the very name he gives it.

**Two readings of *shadīd*.** Ibn Kathir reports two opinions about what "he is *shadīd*" means: that he is **severe in his love of wealth**, or that he is **covetous and stingy due to the love of wealth**. His verdict: "both views are correct." One describes the pull inward toward acquiring; the other describes the clamped fist that will not let go. In practice they are the same disease facing two directions.

**And notice how ayah 8 sits with ayah 6.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the passage exactly this way: having taken the oath by war-horses, the subject states two points — first, that man is ungrateful, "a blamer of his Lord who remembers misfortunes and forgets His favours"; and second, that he is passionate in his love for wealth. Both points, it says, are evil "rationally as well as from the Shari'ah point of view," and these statements warn man against these evils.

## What exactly is being condemned — and what is not

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here, and this is the most practically important passage in the whole commentary on these ayat. It observes that the evil of ingratitude is quite obvious and needs no elaboration, but the evil of man's violent love for wealth is not that obvious and does need it. Why? Because:

> Wealth is the axis of man's needs and necessities. Shari'ah has not only permitted its acquisition, but it has also made its acquisition obligatory to the degree of his needs.

So this is not a surah against earning. Working for what you and your dependants need is not merely allowed — it is a duty. What ayah 8 condemns, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is one of two things:

1. **The "intense" or excessive love** for wealth "that makes one neglectful to one's obligations, and oblivious of the divine injunctions"; or
2. **The love itself lodging in the heart** — that earning wealth, and even saving it according to one's needs, is permissible, but having its love in the heart is bad.

The measure, then, is not the size of the bank balance. It is what your wealth is doing to your obligations and to your heart.

## Two images worth keeping

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a homely illustration to make the distinction concrete. When a person feels the need to answer the call of nature, he does it out of necessity, and in fact makes arrangements for it — but he does not develop love or passion for it in his heart. Likewise when he falls sick and takes medication, or even undergoes surgery: he does it only out of necessity and forms no attachment to it. **The believer should treat wealth in this way**: acquire it, as Allah has commanded, to the extent of his need, save it, look after it and use it whenever and wherever necessary — "but his heart should not be attached to it."

Then it quotes a verse of Maulana Rumi:

> "As long as the water remains under the boat, it helps the boat [to sail]; but if the water seeps into the boat, it sinks it."

And it applies it: as long as wealth floats *around* the boat of the heart it is useful; when it seeps *into* the heart, it destroys it. The same water. The only question is which side of the hull it is on.

## Where the passage is heading

These three ayat are a charge sheet, and the surah does not leave it hanging. Ibn Kathir observes that Allah then "encourages abstinence from worldly things and striving for the Hereafter," informing us of what the situation will be after this present condition and what man will face of horrors. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise notes that towards the conclusion of the surah a warning is sounded against these two evil qualities of man, for which he will be punished in the Hereafter.

That is the logic of the passage: what your heart loves is not, in the end, a private matter.

## Living it

Read against ayat 6–8, the practical questions are narrow and searching:

- **Which ledger do you keep?** Al-Hasan's *kanūd* counts the calamities and forgets Allah's favours. Try reversing the count deliberately — name the mercies before the grievances.
- **Where do your eyes stop?** In the saying Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Tirmidhi, the ungrateful man looks at the bounty and not at the Bounteous Lord. Gratitude means letting the gift point past itself.
- **What is the bounty being spent on?** Abu Bakr Wasiti's definition asks whether Allah's gifts are being spent for sinful purposes.
- **Is your wealth under the boat or in it?** Earning and saving to the measure of your need is commanded. Attachment is the leak. Watch for the tell Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names: when love of wealth starts making you "neglectful to one's obligations, and oblivious of the divine injunctions," the water is already inside.

And behind all of it, ayah 7: whichever way the pronoun is read — Allah as witness, or man as witness against himself — the case is not in doubt. The only thing still open is what we do about it.

passages.title: Graves emptied, hearts exposed before the Lord
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat close Sūrah al-ʿĀdiyāt by putting a single sobering question to man: does he really not know what is coming? Ayat 9 and 10 name two upheavals of the Last Day — the graves emptied of their contents, and the contents of the hearts brought out into the open — and ayah 11 seals both with the reason none of it can go wrong: **their Lord, on that Day, is fully aware of them.**

What holds the three together is a movement from the outside inward, and then upward. First what the earth was hiding is turned out (ayah 9). Then what the chest was hiding is turned out (ayah 10). Then the One before whom all of it is laid bare is named (ayah 11). Ibn Kathir titles this section of the surah **"The Threat about the Hereafter,"** and explains that here Allah "encourages abstinence from worldly things and striving for the Hereafter," informing man "of what the situation will be after this present condition, and what man will face of horrors."

## The question that carries the whole passage

Ayah 9 does not begin with a statement but with a question: *Afalā yaʿlam* — "Does he not then know?" (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān), "Knows he not?" (Ibn Kathir).

A question put like this is not seeking information. Ibn Kathir reads the whole passage as a *threat* — a warning — and that tells us what the question is doing: it confronts. The "he" being addressed is the man the surah has just been describing. Ibn Kathir explains of him that "he (man) is ungrateful for the favors of His Lord and he rejects them," and that "in his love of the good, which is wealth, he is severe." The question exposes the gap between what such a person knows and how such a person lives. He is not being told something new; he is being asked why what he already knows is having no effect on him.

That is why the passage lands with force. The surah has just finished describing a heart bent double over wealth. Now it turns that heart towards the one scene in which wealth is of no use at all — the day the graves give up what is in them.

## Ayah 9: the graves turned out

Ibn Kathir's gloss on this ayah is stripped down and physical: **"meaning, the dead that are in it will be brought out."** His rendering is that the contents of the graves are **"poured forth."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it as **"overturned"** — "when all that is contained in the graves will be overturned."

Both renderings carry the same picture: a container tipped up and emptied out. The graves are not opened politely; their contents are turned out of them.

And notice how the ayah speaks — not "when the dead come out," but "when *what is in* the graves is poured forth." The dead are named as *contents*, as what a place is holding, until the moment the holding ends. Hold onto that word "contents." The very next ayah uses it again.

## Ayah 10: the chests turned out

The second upheaval is the more searching one, and the wording is built so that you feel it is the *same* act performed on a different container. What is in the graves is turned out; what is in the chests is turned out. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering keeps the parallel exactly: "all that is contained in the graves will be overturned, and all that is contained in the hearts will be exposed."

Ibn Kathir renders it, **"And that which is in the breasts shall be made known,"** and reports from **Ibn ʿAbbās and others**: **"This means what was in their souls would be exposed and made apparent."**

Sit with what that means. The grave holds a body that no one can see; the chest holds an inner life that no one can see. In this world both are sealed. A person can be read only by what he lets out — his words, his face, his public deeds — and every one of those can be managed. What is in the chest is the part of us we have never had to show anyone: the real motive under the generous act, the calculation under the kind word, the resentment we kept indoors, the sincerity no one ever gave us credit for.

Ayah 10 says that this too has a day of being emptied out. And in a passage aimed at a man who "is severe" in his love of wealth, this is precisely the strike that lands. Greed is one of the sins most easily dressed up. It can be called prudence, ambition, responsibility, providing for the family. Ayah 10 announces the end of dressing anything up — not merely that deeds will be listed, but that what was *in the souls* will be "exposed and made apparent." The presentable version of a life will not survive that day.

There is also a mercy hidden in the same sentence, and it should not be missed. If the chests are turned out, then what was in them that was *good* is turned out too. Every private prayer no one witnessed, every quiet restraint, every unwitnessed intention to please Allah alone — the same exposure that exposes the pretender vindicates the sincere. Ibn Kathir draws out this side when he comes to ayah 11: Allah "knows all of that they used to do, and He will compensate them for it with the most deserving reward."

## Ayah 11: their Lord, that Day, is fully aware

The final ayah is the ground under both of the others: "Verily, that Day their Lord will be Well-Acquainted with them" (Ibn Kathir); "Surely your Lord, that day, is fully aware of them" (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān).

Two things in this ayah repay attention.

**First, the shift from "he" to "them."** The preceding ayat spoke of *man* in the singular — he is ungrateful, he is severe in his love of wealth, does *he* not know. Ayah 11 speaks in the plural: *their* Lord, aware of *them*. The individual indictment opens out into the crowd standing on that Day. Every single "he" the surah has been describing is there, all at once, all known.

**Second, "their Lord."** This is the same word the surah used when it laid its charge: "man is ungrateful *to his Lord*," where, as Ibn Kathir explains, he "is ungrateful for the favors of His Lord and he rejects them." The charge and the verdict are pinned to the same relationship. The favours he was ungrateful for came from Him; the reckoning comes from Him too. Ingratitude here is not an offence against a stranger.

Ibn Kathir renders the closing word "Well-Acquainted"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "fully aware." Ibn Kathir explains: **"meaning, He knows all of that they used to do, and He will compensate them for it with the most deserving reward. He does not do even the slightest amount of injustice."** Maʿārif draws the same conclusion: "Divine retribution will be meted out, in the Hereafter, to each person commensurate with his deeds, good or bad, as Allah is well-aware of them."

And here is the quiet logic of the passage. Why speak of Allah's awareness *on that Day* when His knowledge of what they used to do is not something the Day produces? Because ayat 9 and 10 have just described the day everything becomes visible **to creation**, and this ayah tells us that none of that exposure is a discovery **for Allah**. The turning out of the graves and the turning out of the chests reveal to us what was never hidden from Him. That is exactly why the judgement can be perfectly exact — "He does not do even the slightest amount of injustice."

## Who exactly is "man" here?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on an important question about these verses. They describe "these evil qualities of man in general terms" — yet the Prophets (ʿalayhim as-salām), the friends of Allah and many of His righteous servants are free of them. They "acquire wealth through lawful means and abstain from acquiring it through unlawful means," are "ever so grateful to Allah for the wealth He has given them," and "spend it in the way of Allah." So how can such faults be attributed to man in general terms?

The answer Maʿārif gives is that **most** people have these qualities, "but this does not imply that all, without any exception, are characterized by these qualities. The upright people are excluded from the general statement." It further notes that **some of the scholars restrict the word "man" here to "unbelievers,"** since these two qualities "are the essential characteristics of unbelievers." And then it adds the line every Muslim reader should take personally: if they are found in a Muslim, "he needs to reflect and be careful." Maʿārif closes, as the scholars do, with **"Allah knows best!"**

That note protects the passage from two misreadings. It is not a blanket condemnation of humanity, and it is not a description of someone else. It is a mirror handed to whoever is reading.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical conclusion itself, and it is worth quoting as the sum of the passage: because Allah is well-aware and repayment is exactly commensurate with deeds, **"it would be wise for man to abstain from ingratitude, and he should not have such a violently passionate love for wealth and indulgence in worldly riches as to be unable to separate the good from the bad."**

Notice the precise harm named there. The danger of loving wealth too fiercely is not only that it makes a person stingy — it is that it *blinds the judgement*, until he can no longer separate the good from the bad. A heart in that state has lost its instrument for the very reckoning ayah 11 promises.

So the passage asks three concrete things.

**Refuse ingratitude.** Ibn Kathir preserves al-Ḥasan's description of the ungrateful man — *al-kanūd* — as **"the one who counts the calamities (that befall him) and he forgets Allah's favors."** Ayah 10 says the inner tally will one day be brought out; make it run the other way now, while it is still private.

**Take your inner life as seriously as your outer one.** Ayah 10 says the chest is a container that will be emptied out and "made apparent." The honest question is not "how does this look?" but "what is actually in here?"

**Keep wealth in the hands, not the chest.** Maʿārif's portrait of the righteous is not that they have no wealth, but that they take it lawfully, are grateful to Allah for it, and spend it in His way.

Ibn Kathir ends his commentary on the surah with the line that should be our last word too: Allah "will compensate them for it with the most deserving reward. He does not do even the slightest amount of injustice."
